SPREAD SPECTRUM MODULATION
OBJECTIVES
w Identify the different techniques of spread spectrum modulation.
w Define and explain the purpose of spread spectrum modulation.
w Describe the PN sequence generation in spread spectrum systems.
w Describe the need and process for synchronization and preamble in spread spectrum systems.......................................

Austrian actress Hedy Lamarr and American composer George Antheil developed a method of radio communications that takes the transmitted signal and distributes it over a large band of ever changing frequencies, thereby making the torpedo control signal undetectable and unjammable...

The system is called spread spectrum and Lamarr and Antheil shared a 1942 U.S. patent for the innovation. At the time, the technology to produce such a system was unavailable and so languished beneath layers of Federal bureaucracy until 1963. When transistors were introduced, Lamarr's vision came of age...

With the rapid growth of the world population and technologies that become cheaper by the day, the demand placed on the RF spectrum will increase proportionately. In many undeveloped countries, where only minimal landline telephone systems exist, cellular telephones outnumber land-based telephones...

In Japan, there are more cellular telephones than conventional telephones. Wireless computer networks are rapidly growing and using spread spectrum modulation schemes. The advantages of spread spectrum systems in such an environment make the likelihood of it becoming obsolete very slim...
Let's begin the lesson on SPREAD SPECTRUM MODULATION......................
LESSON MENU
SPREAD SPECTRUM MODULATION

A spread spectrum (SS) communications system can be defined as one which spreads the average energy of the transmitted signal over a bandwidth that is much wider than the information bandwidth, and uses some signal or operation (other than the intelligence being sent) to spread the transmitted signal...
DISCUSSION

The useful energy in a conventional amplitude modulated, frequency modulated, or pulse modulated signal is concentrated around a center frequency. The efficiency of these and other modulation schemes is often equated with how tightly they concentrate signal energy for a given information rate...

Spread spectrum modulation techniques take the opposite approach- that of spreading the signal out over a very wide bandwidth. Radio-frequency bandwidths that greatly exceed the bandwidth necessary to convey the intelligence are used...
Communications signals can be largely increased in bandwidth by factors of 10 to 10,000 by combining them with binary sequences (PN code) using several techniques that will be described later...

Bandwidths for SS systems generally run from 10 to 100 times the information rate. By spreading the power over a wide band, the amount of energy in any particular frequency is very much smaller than for conventional narrow-band modulation techniques...

Depending upon the transmitter power level, the distance from the transmitter to the receiver and the width of the spread signal, the SS signal may be below the noise level of a conventional receiver. It would then be invisible to it, while it can be received with a spread spectrum receiver...

SS systems also use code sequences to modulate and demodulate the transmission. Only the intended receiver (or receivers in a net operation) can recover the signal, as both sender and receiver hold copies of the binary sequence that is used to spread the signal and know where in the sequence the code was initiated.....

Receivers with the wrong code will not be able to demodulate the encoded SS signal and will be highly immune to interference from it. Receivers with the correct code are able to add all the spread energy in a constructive way to reproduce the intended information...

The receiver can reject strong undesired signals, even those much stronger than the desired spread spectrum signal power density. This is because the desired receiver has a copy of the spreading sequence that it uses to reassemble the signal. Nonspread signals are then rejected in the processing...

Interference to other users of the same spectrum is little or none (unless they are close to the transmitter). The effectiveness of spread spectrum's interference-rejection property has made it a popular military antijamming technique...

Spread spectrum's inherent security benefits greatly interested the military, not just for control signals of torpedoes and missiles, but also for communications. During the years of the 50's, 60's, and 70's, the military worked with spread spectrum but held most of its development in secrecy...

From the civilian perspective, not only were the security benefits attractive, but the efficiency that spread spectrum technology demonstrated in its use of the RF spectrum was unsurpassed by conventional modulation techniques...

By the 1980's, with the introduction of cellular telephony, the demand put upon the RF spectrum grew and is continuing to grow today. Spread spectrum is ideally tailored for cellular telephone systems allowing multiple, low-power transmissions to occupy the same set of frequencies, sometimes simultaneously.....

Effective spectrum management allows the greatest use of a band of frequencies by the largest number of possible users. This permits more users in densely populated areas that would normally have been using up a far greater slice of the total available spectrum...

Spread spectrum can be used in precise ranging and radar systems. The PN modulated spread carrier allows the receiver to accurately measure the time the signal was sent, therefore, the signal can be used to time the distance to a transmitter for ranging, or to an object for radar reflection...

SS can also make use of unused portions of a frequency band such as between repeater channels. Spread spectrum technology is also used in wireless LAN systems, pagers, and range measuring for radar and the Global Positioning Systems...

There are, fundamentally, four methods to generate a spread spectrum signal:
Of the four methods, direct sequence and frequency hopping are the most commonly used by the telecommunications industry. Hybrid forms can be produced by combining two or more of the methods...

The most common form of spread spectrum is direct sequence and it is typically used to transmit digital information. The signal is produced by modulating the intelligence signal with a binary sequence generated by a shift register with feedback connections...

It's called a pseudo-noise (PN) code because the sequence has many characteristics of noise, hence, the N. The PN code is a high-speed sequence of 1's and 0's often called chips. The sequence of 1's and 0's appears to be random but is, in fact, a sequence that repeats itself over a very long period of time...

The simplest version is a carrier that is switched between two phases that are 180 degrees apart in accordance with the PN code. The receiver tracks these pseudo-random phase inversions by using a stored copy of the pattern. For this system to work, the receiver must use the exact PN code as the transmitter.....

The information signal is multiplied by the chip sequence at the transmitter, which expands the bandwidth beyond the information bandwidth. The receiver restores the signal to the information bandwidth by re-multiplying it with the PN code. This reverts the intelligence signal back to its original form...

The mixing is accomplished by an Exclusive NOR function that multiplies the intelligence and PN code together. The output of the Exclusive NOR gate section is then modulated with the carrier frequency, amplified, and sent to the antenna...

Interference is subjected to one multiplication process (this occurs in the receiver) so its bandwidth is increased to the bandwidth of the chip waveform. The receiver filters the interference energy from the information bandwidth...
Spread spectrum generated through frequency hopping (FH) is similar to direct sequence in that this scheme also requires a PN code; but that is where the similarity ends.

Frequency hopping is a method where the operating frequency is changed rapidly over the spread bandwidth. Both transmitter and receiver visit the same frequencies at the same time and must remain synchronized...

Each has the same list of pseudorandom-ordered frequencies, and they start hopping together using the same starting point on the list. If the receiver is out of step with the signal, it cannot recover the information being transmitted...

The amount of time the signal spends on any single channel is called dwell time and is commonly less than 10 milliseconds. The short dwell time is to avoid interference to and from conventional users of the hopped channels...

At any instant in time, a frequency hopping transmitter is emitting all of its power on a specific frequency and there is potential for interference with someone else using a narrow-band system on that frequency. The FH dwell time on that particular frequency is so short that it will not be noticeable to most narrow-band users...

It may be convenient to classify the systems as fast or slow hopping. The rate of a fast hopping system is significantly greater than the information rate. Slow-hopping systems have a hopping rate equal to or less than the information rate...
Fast Hop System - Hopping Rate > Information Rate
Slow Hop System - Hopping Rate > Information Rate

Where the PN code was multiplied with the intelligence in direct sequence, in frequency hopping the intelligence is first conventionally modulated creating an intermediate frequency (IF)...

The PN code is fed through a logic control circuit to a local oscillator (frequency synthesizer). This causes the synthesizer to hop from one carrier frequency to another. Hopping rates may be determined by circuit considerations, such as how long it takes a particular frequency synthesizer to settle at a new frequency.....

The upconverter mixes the IF with the random carrier frequencies (RF) and its output is fed to an amplifier prior to being transmitted. The frequencies hopped to within the given band are of equal amplitude...
The bandwidth of the final frequency-hopping signal is determined by multiplying the total number of hopped frequencies by the bandwidth of each hop frequency.
If there are N separate hopping frequencies, each being used for an equal fraction of the transmission time, then the interference power is reduced by a factor of N when averaged over all hops.

Processing gain for frequency hop signals refers to a gain approximated by the ratio of the RF bandwidth to the information bandwidth. Processing gain may reduce interference signals by as much as 40 dB...
For example, a signal with a 100 MHz RF bandwidth and an information bandwidth of 10 KHz has a processing gain of
40 dB. Processing Gain = 100 MHz/10 kHz = 10,000 = 10 LOG 10,000 = 40 dB. Thus, the output signal- to-noise ratio is 40 dB higher than the receiver input signal-to-noise ratio.

The pulse-FM (chirp) process of SS generation is similar to frequency hopping in that the frequency is varied. The difference is that in pulsed-FM systems the carrier frequency is altered linearly across the entire bandwidth at a known rate as opposed to varying discrete frequencies as in frequency hopping systems.....

The process is similar to a signal produced by a sweep generator. Conventional modulation of the swept carrier by the intelligence signal is then used. Pure chirp systems do not use a code sequence to influence the sweep time, which is normally independent of the intelligence...

At the receiver, a matched filter is employed to compress the signal to a much narrower band. Pulse - FM is regularly used by ranging and radar systems and has little use in most commercial communication spread spectrum systems...

The last major form of spread spectrum is called time hopping and operates much the same way as frequency hopping except that the variants occur in the time domain rather than the frequency domain. The graphic illustrates six different users on the same frequency and only one can transmit during each time frame.....

This method is a form of pulse modulation using a code sequence to control the pulse. The carrier signal is on-off keyed by the PN sequence. Like other pulse-based systems, transmitter activity is not constant and the duty cycle may be as low as 50%. The speed of keying determines how much the signal is spread.....

The signal from the transmitter is propagated in very short time intervals. The length of each interval is based upon a pseudo-random code like those used in direct sequence and frequency hopping. The sequence of transmission times is stored in the receiver so that re-creation of the original signal is possible...

There are hybrid systems that combine two or more of the four basic methods to create a system far less vulnerable to security invasions. They also can produce results with higher performance than when the methods are employed in their pure form...
One of the most critical components of any spread spectrum system is the PN sequence used to spread the RF carrier. PN codes are used for spreading the intelligence over a wide band of frequencies...
The PN code reflects the type of spread spectrum generation that is being used, and it determines how well the properties of the signal perform.

In direct sequence generation, the PN code is a very fast, digitally-generated bit stream used to shift the phase of the carrier; whereas in frequency hopping, the binary chips (bits) represent the channels that the signal will hop to...

Many ways exist to generate the PN code sequence. The most common method creates a group of code sequences called maximal linear code sequences or M-sequences. These sequences are the longest codes producible by a linear-feedback shift register (LFSR) of some given size...

The shift register consists of a number of one-bit memory registers (flip-flops) that shift their contents to the right with each clock pulse. New values are introduced at the left-most stage and the output is usually taken from the right-most stage. The shift register can be used to generate a wide variety of sequences......
Generation of a linear sequence is done by tapping the values of certain cells and combining the values by an Exclusive-OR gate. The combined output becomes the input of the left-most cell.

The LFSR sequence repeats itself and the maximum length is directly related to the number of stages (N) in the shift register by the equation: length= 2(N-1). Not all tap choices produce the longest sequence. An entire repeating sequence is considered a cycle...

For example, a 16-bit (216) register, produces 65,536 unique numerical combinations. An 8-bit (28) register can produce 256 unique numerical combinations. The generator can begin with any number from the sequence, but commonly, the register is preloaded (initiated) with all zeros followed by a one...
7486 has an inverter to make an exclusive NOR function.

The sequence is then allowed to begin. Since the inputs to the Exclusive OR gate are taken from two separate stages of the register, the generated 1s and 0s are not counting in a conventional manner; rather, the sequence of numbers appears random...
When the feedback tap outputs are 0 and the output of the XOR stage is 0, the input to the shift register is 0. This arrangement is a nonallowable state and the shift register hangs up.
7486 has an inverter to make an exclusive NOR function.

When an inverter stage is added to one section of the quad XOR gate, the 0 output from the XOR stage, obtained on reset, is now a 1 and the counting sequence can begin again. This creates an Exclusive Nor function...

In a hypothetical example, a four-bit operation might generate the numbers: 1000, 0100, 0010, and 1001 and so on, depending upon which stages (flip-flop outputs) were selected for the inputs to the Exclusive OR gate..
4 Bit-shift-keyed PN sequence with 3.4 stages tapped

The graphic lists a complete PN sequence (with decimal equivalents) generated by a four bit-shift-keyed register that taps flip-flop 3 and flip-flop 4. A four-stage register allows for 16 (24) unique numbers. One output is not shown as it would make the output constant and not change...
Other more complex code sequences can be created by having two M-sequence generators whose outputs are combined by an Exclusive OR function. These are called Gold Codes.

The most demanding issue in designing and implementing a spread spectrum system is synchronizing the receiver with the transmitter. If synchronization is not achieved, even just one bit off, nothing but noise is heard...

In order for the spread spectrum receiver to demodulate an incoming signal, it must first know the PN sequence being used by the transmitter. It must also be able to either synchronize itself to the starting point in the PN sequence or align itself to whatever point the sequence is in at the time of reception...

This process can be viewed as having two stages. First, rough synchronization, in which the receiver endeavors to align its own PN code as closely as possible to the transmitter's code (usually within one bit of the transmitter's)...

The second stage is fine synchronization where the receiver maintains bit timing or channel dwell time. Channel dwell time refers to frequency hopping and is the amount of time that the signal remains at one channel before hopping to the next...
Rough synchronization is normally achieved by one of two methods: Epoch Synchronization or Phase Synchronization.

In the epoch system, the transmitter communicates a reference time mark that identifies the occurrence of a particular instant of time such as the beginning of a sequence, or as they are often called, unique words, to a receiver...

This is done in the time domain by periodically sending a unique word or sequence that can be easily detected by a digital matched filter. These filters are called correlators and consists of a shift register. The register shifts the received sequence one bit at a time and compares the output to a unique sequence..

A correlator compares the similarity of two signals and identifies signals with the desired spreading code. It is actually performing a despreading process, which will isolate the original digital information that is the intelligence being sent...

In phase synchronization, the receiver identifies the location of the 2(N-1) phase of the M-sequence. This determination is established when N (a pre-determined number) bits are received without error...
The actual number is pre-established by the system and code being used. If the ambient noise levels are too high, the number of bits required for synchronization increases.

For systems having the same bandwidth, frequency hopping system receivers usually synchronize with the transmitted signal within a fraction of a second and direct sequence systems can require a second or more. Short synchronization time is desirable in voice communications...

If one or two seconds is required for synchronization, the transmitter must be keyed a couple of seconds before voice is received. Therefore, a voice reply could be delayed by two seconds, which may not be acceptable. No noticeable delay would occur in a frequency hopping signal...

A preamble signal is normally sent prior to the transmitter entering the spread mode. The preamble is a signal sent by the transmitter that notifies the receiver to prepare its synchronization procedure to receive a spread spectrum transmission. The composition of the signal varies from system to system.....
Spread spectrum technology offers an extensive sharing of frequencies with minimal interference, which enhances the possibilities for use in the telecommunications industry.
